text: All day long, fluid slips out of your tiniest blood vessels and into your tissues. If it had nowhere to go, you would swell up. So where does the fluid go? Let's find out.
The answer is your lymphatic system. It is a network of vessels, nodes and organs. The fluid it carries is called lymph. It starts as interstitial fluid, the fluid between your cells.

Tiny lymphatic capillaries absorb that extra fluid. It becomes lymph, flows through lymphatic vessels, and is returned to the bloodstream through large veins near the collarbone, called the subclavian veins. That is the mystery solved. The lymphatic system drains your tissues.
Lymph has no heart to push it. Valves in the vessels keep it moving one way, and the squeezing of nearby muscles helps push it along.

Along the way, lymph passes through lymph nodes. You have about six hundred of them. They filter the lymph, remove debris and germs, and contain lymphocytes. When you have an infection, nearby nodes can swell.
Other lymphatic organs help too. The spleen filters your blood. The thymus is where T cells mature. And the tonsils help block germs that try to enter your body.
In the small intestine, special lymph capillaries called lacteals help absorb dietary fats.

If lymph cannot drain, because of a blockage or damaged vessels or nodes, fluid builds up. This swelling is called lymphedema, and it most often affects the arms or legs. If you notice unexplained swelling or a lump, see a doctor.

Remember three things. The lymphatic system drains fluid from your tissues and returns it to the blood. Lymph nodes filter lymph and house immune cells. And lacteals help absorb fats. Next time, the senses: how your eyes turn light into sight.
